summary: Polis plays like a tight economic engine-management game wearing a wargame's clothes: most of the tension comes from feeding your population, running trade routes to five markets, and husbanding scarce prestige, with actual battles being infrequent but pivotal set pieces. It is widely described as brutally unforgiving of mismanagement, where a single misstep in logistics, iron, or prestige can end the game outright long before the map is settled.
praised: Elegant, tightly balanced design that fuses euro-style economic engine-building with a light wargame
High component and production quality, including a double-layered board
Strong thematic cohesion between trade, feeding your population, diplomacy, and war
Deep strategy emerging from a compact, minimalist ruleset with little tedium
Genuine tension since combat, market access, and diplomacy directly interfere with the opponent
criticised: Very unforgiving/punishing: no safety nets, and new players often lose outright to starvation, running out of prestige, or a botched attack rather than losing on points
Steep learning curve best learned by losing a few times
Fixed setup and limited variability between plays compared to modern asymmetric designs
Surprisingly little actual fighting for a game themed around the Peloponnesian War
Games can end abruptly and early (after any of four eras) if a player collapses economically, which some find anticlimactic

interaction.kind: direct military conflict and diplomacy over shared territories
interaction.detail: As a two-player wargame, players fight over control of the same territories via combat and sieges, and can also try to diplomatically flip a rival's polis to their side, directly taking something from the opponent. Supply routes and markets are likewise contested rather than personal, so most of the game state is shared and fought over.

scoring.how_you_win: Grow and feed your population across controlled territory, trade at the five markets, and fight or negotiate for rival territory; the empire with the greater combined population and prestige at the end wins.

similar: COIN series games (e.g. Gandhi, All Bridges Burning)

theme.said: unknown — thin BGG presence, but description reads as fairly standard civ-lite area control with an economic layer bolted on
theme.why: needing to feed the population you control before it produces goods, and being able to woo a rival polis to defect through diplomacy rather than only combat, are rules that plainly derive from real city-state politics rather than being generic filler

style.why: A market-and-supply economy is contested directly through dice-resolved battles and sieges between two civilizations, blending trade with war.
